newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila sugar industry welcomes halt on tariff cut.
newsitem.headline: Manila sugar industry welcomes halt on tariff cut.

text.p: Manila's decision to halt a tariff cut on imported Southeast Asian sugar will give the battered sugar industry a reprieve, officials and industry executives said on Wednesday.
"It's welcome news. However, the two-year reprieve is not enough to provide stability of investments," said Jose Maria Zabaleta, executive director of the Philippine Sugar Mills Association.
"But what's important is the government has clearly indicated its willingness to rejuvenate this industry," Zabaleta added.

President Fidel Ramos, in an executive order signed on June 17 but only made public on Wednesday, ordered the country's tariff on imported sugar from the Association of South East Asian Nations be maintained at 65 percent for two years starting on July 1.
Earlier, as part of its commitment to the ASEAN Free Trade agreement, Manila had decided to cut the tariff to 52.5 percent starting on July 1.
ASEAN groups Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines.
Philippine sugar farmers and millers had complained that the planned tariff cut would kill the local sugar industry.
Manila has been swamped by imported sugar, mostly from Thailand, in recent months resulting in a glut.
The government can negotiate with Southeast Asian countries to maintain its tariff for a few more years depending on market conditions, said Agriculture Secretary Salvador Escudero.
"The government needs to provide certain agricultural sectors interim tariff adjustments to help the sector to be efficient and globally competitive," the order signed by Ramos said.

Zabaleta said the Philippine sugar sector is threatened by an "unenlightened government policy that may force prices too low through a policy of importation and low tariffs from the unpredictable and volatile world market."
Once a top sugar exporter, Manila is now an importer due to years of complacency and its inability to compete with more efficient sugar producers, analysts said.

"Uncertainty rules at present, if not fear, as a result of bankruptcies of some mills and the foreseeable bankruptcies of so many farms," Zabaleta said in a speech on the prospects of the Philippine sugar industry at the University of Asia and the Pacific on Tuesday.

The Philippine's largest sugar mill, Victorias Milling Corp and its trading arm, have asked for a moratorium from banks on their combined debts worth more than six billion pesos recently due to the slump in the industry.
Zabaleta said the sugar crisis was a result of outdated farming practices, lack of new technologies to improve productivity, and insuffient funding.

Banks no longer lend for equipment and inputs for land improvements as sugar lands lost their collateral value due to the government's land redistribution programme that broke up large sugar plantations.
"Where land reform has taken place, indebted beneficiaries cannot borrow more or don't even know how to secure adequate financing (for farm improvement)," he said.
